description: A group of high school and technical students in Guatemala working to integrate technology into everyday local contexts.Driven by an interest in software and practical digital tools, the team aims to propose technological alternatives to existing problems in their environment, focusing on simple, direct solutions that can bring gradual improvements to their community.
summary:
I wanted to grow corn on my land in Guatemala, but I didn't know if I could, when to plant, or what the weather would do to it. Millions of small farmers live with that same doubt, and one long dry spell or a storm can wipe out a whole season. That's why our team chose Field Shift.

We built SeedView, a free web app where anyone, anywhere in the world, finds their land on a 3D globe, draws their field and picks a crop. SeedView simulates the whole season with NASA POWER data and tells you if the crop can really be harvested there (and why not, if it can't), the best date to plant, the risk of losing the harvest, and what to do each day of the year. You can watch your season grow in 3D, day by day, before planting a single seed. Alerts for storms, dry spells, frost and heat arrive on WhatsApp, the app farmers already use.

We also built SEED, our own IoT field sensor, an ESP32-S3 with a soil moisture probe that measures how wet the soil really is, right in the field. We don't just simulate. We join NASA's data with real readings from the soil, so every forecast gets more accurate.

SeedView doesn't replace the farmer's knowledge. It puts space data in their pocket so they can decide with less risk.
details:
The story

I wanted to grow corn on my land in Guatemala. I had the land and the will, but I didn't know if corn would actually grow there, when I should plant it, or what the weather was going to do during the season. Asking around, I realized almost every small farmer plants the same way: by tradition and by luck. In Guatemala, a long canícula (mid-summer dry spell), a tropical storm or an early frost can destroy a whole harvest, and climate change is making those seasons harder to predict. We chose the Field Shift challenge because we wanted anyone, anywhere in the world, to be able to know before they sow.

What SeedView does

  • Find and draw your field. You open SeedView, search your village or neighbourhood (or use your GPS) on a 3D globe, zoom in to your land and draw its outline. The size is estimated automatically and you can edit it.
  • Pick a crop, get a recommendation. You choose milpa (corn and beans), corn or beans, and SeedView tells you which one has the lowest risk on that exact spot and why. For now SeedView works with three crops only: milpa, corn and beans.
  • Can it really grow here? If the crop can't be harvested there, SeedView says it clearly and explains the reason: too dry, too cold, frost, heat, or the season is too short for it to mature.
  • Watch your season in 3D. Before planting a single seed, you can watch your field grow day by day in a 3D simulation with real NASA weather: rain, dry spells, the plants growing, and the harvest (or the loss).
  • A plan for every day. Your field gets a dashboard with the best planting date, the expected harvest date, a week / month / year calendar with what to do each day (water, weed, fertilize, watch for pests), how much water your field needs today, and the risk of losing the harvest. You can use it without an account, and create a free one to save your fields.
  • Alerts on WhatsApp. Farmers already use WhatsApp, so that's where SeedView talks to them. When you link your number, the bot greets you by your field's name, sends the 3D video of your season and this week's plan, and then warns you about storms, hurricanes, dry spells, frost, extreme heat and pests. You can also ask it questions like "will it rain on October 20?".
  • SEED, our IoT sensor. We designed and 3D-printed SEED: an ESP32-S3 board with an HW-080 soil moisture probe that measures how wet the soil really is, right next to the plants. It sends its readings over WiFi to SeedView, which compares the expected season (NASA-based simulation) with what is actually happening in the field, so the plan adapts. The firmware can be installed and configured straight from the browser over USB.

How it works

Our team defined everything, from the idea to the structure and the infrastructure, and we built the project with the help of artificial intelligence, specifically Claude Opus 5.5 by Anthropic. At the core is a deterministic agronomic engine. It downloads daily NASA POWER data for the field (temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation, rain and root-zone soil wetness, 2001 to today), computes reference evapotranspiration with FAO-56 Penman-Monteith, runs a daily crop water balance, and estimates yield loss from water stress with FAO-33. It replays hundreds of past seasons (Monte Carlo over the NASA record, weighted by El Niño / La Niña analogs from NOAA's ONI) to give the probability of losing the harvest for each planting date, then picks the best one. Crop thermal limits decide if the crop can survive and mature at that location. The next 16 days use a weather forecast; beyond that, the simulation uses the historical NASA climate. Satellite layers (MODIS vegetation and temperature, GPM IMERG rain, Sentinel-2) help the farmer see their land, and SRTM elevation builds the 3D terrain. We back-tested the alert system on the 2026 season in Jocotán (Dry Corridor): 5 of 6 dry-spell alerts were confirmed by observed rain, with no false alarms.

Benefits and impact

A farmer who knows the risk before planting can change the date, the crop or the plan instead of losing their seed, water and work. SeedView turns complex satellite and climate data into simple decisions: "plant on this date", "water this much today", "this crop won't make it here". It is free, works in the browser on any phone, speaks Spanish and English, and reaches people through WhatsApp. We hope it helps reduce lost harvests and food insecurity, starting in Guatemala, where millions of people face hunger after bad seasons, and growing to any farm in the world.

Tools we used

Go (backend and engine, also compiled to WebAssembly), Vue 3 + TypeScript + Vite (web app), MapLibre GL (3D globe and maps), three.js (3D season simulation and sensor model), SQLite, FFmpeg with GPU encoding (3D season videos for WhatsApp), Evolution API (WhatsApp), ESP32-S3 with Arduino (SEED firmware), ESP Web Tools (flashing from the browser), OpenSCAD and a 3D printer (SEED enclosure), HW-080 soil moisture probe, Vercel and Cloudflare (hosting). Code: https://github.com/Astral910/ArasakaT

What makes it creative

Instead of showing farmers charts, SeedView lets them see their own season before it happens, in 3D, on their own land, and then follows them through WhatsApp with a real sensor in the ground checking that the forecast matches reality. Space data, a local sensor and the chat app people already use, working together.

What we considered

Most small farmers don't have a computer, but almost all of them have a phone, and WhatsApp is usually the app they use the most. That's why SeedView works in the phone's browser and talks to farmers on WhatsApp. They also don't have time to read data, so every screen ends in a decision, not a number. SeedView supports their knowledge and their local extension agent, never replaces them. We designed it to work anywhere in the world, not just in Guatemala.

We don't just simulate. We join NASA's data with real readings from the soil, so every forecast gets more accurate.
